title: How to Calculate Landed Margin on Syncee Products Before You List Them
excerpt: A landed margin worksheet for marketplace-sourced products: supplier price, shipping tiers, payment fees, return allowance, and the break-even ad cost you can actually afford.
body: Most margin problems in marketplace sourcing are accounting problems rather than pricing problems. A product that looks like a forty percent gross margin on the supplier page can arrive at twelve percent contribution margin once shipping tiers, payment fees, and a realistic return allowance are applied. The fix is boring: build one landed cost worksheet, run every candidate through it before listing, and refuse to list anything that misses your threshold.

Start with the real supplier cost and not the headline number. In marketplace catalogs the same product often has several supplier offers with different price breaks, shipping origins, and processing times. Record the unit cost at your expected volume, the handling fee if one applies, and the country of origin, which drives both transit time and duty exposure. If two offers differ by a dollar but one ships three weeks closer to your customer, the cheaper one is rarely better.

Add shipping the way the customer will experience it. Pull the actual rate for your main destination, including the second item rate if bundles matter, and decide whether you absorb it, fold it into the price, or charge it separately. Free shipping that is silently baked into a price behaves differently from free shipping with a threshold, and the threshold version is usually the one that raises average order value. Whichever you choose, write the number into the sheet instead of estimating it.

Layer on the costs that show up after checkout. Payment processing on a cross-border order is not the same rate as a domestic one, and currency conversion adds a second bite when you settle in a different currency. Add platform fees, any app cost you attribute per order, and a packaging or insert cost if branding is part of the promise. These are small individually and reliably large in aggregate, which is why they get skipped in spreadsheet-free decisions.

Price in failure before it happens. New products return at a higher rate than proven ones, mis-shipments occur, and a percentage of parcels will go missing. Put a return and refund allowance into the sheet as a fixed percentage of revenue rather than hoping for zero, then add a small support cost per order because every exception consumes someone's time. If the product only works when nothing goes wrong, it is not something to scale with paid traffic.

Only then do the acquisition math. Contribution margin minus your target cost per acquisition is the number that decides whether a product is worth scaling, and it should be calculated after everything above. Work backwards from the margin instead of forwards from a hopeful ad cost: if contribution margin is eleven dollars, you do not have a forty dollar acquisition budget, you have a product that needs organic traffic, email, or a much stronger offer.

Run this worksheet on a shortlist rather than a single item, because patterns show up fast: certain categories never clear the bar, and certain origin and price band combinations always do. The DTCwise Dropshipping category at /category/dropshipping keeps the current shortlist with ratings and pricing, which gives you a useful starting set. The Syncee profile at /tool/syncee covers its catalog model, pricing rules, and supplier automation, so you can see which parts of this calculation the platform already supports.
